annotations.description: Playing Bloodstained Mire instead of Swamp wastes 1 life when cracking the fetch, and the player wants to cast Thoughtseize (costs B) or Faithless Looting (costs R) this turn. If they play Swamp, they can cast Thoughtseize immediately for free (no life from fetch). If they play Bloodstained Mire, they need to crack it (paying 1 life) to get a Swamp to cast Thoughtseize, losing 1 unnecessary life point. The fetch land should be saved for later when color flexibility is actually needed or when revolt for Fatal Push matters. Playing Swamp directly and saving the fetchland preserves life and keeps open the option to trigger revolt with Bloodstained Mire on a future turn when Fatal Push needs to hit a 3-4 mana value creature.

annotations.betterLine: Play Swamp, then cast Thoughtseize targeting the opponent without spending an extra life on a fetch crack. Save Bloodstained Mire for a later turn where revolt for Fatal Push or color fixing is needed.

annotations.description: Playing Swamp instead of using Bloodstained Mire is slightly suboptimal. The player has Faithless Looting in hand which they likely want to cast soon to fill the graveyard for Abhorrent Oculus. By cracking Bloodstained Mire for a Swamp (or Mountain), they would get a permanent leaving the battlefield, enabling Revolt for Fatal Push to hit creatures with mana value 4 or less - relevant against the opponent's potential threats like Atraxa. Additionally, thinning the deck and having the fetch available to crack at instant speed on the opponent's turn provides more flexibility. Playing the Swamp from hand preserves the fetch but wastes the opportunity to keep options open - they should save the Swamp for a turn when they have no fetch to play.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Swamp from hand as their land for the turn.
annotations.betterLine: Crack Bloodstained Mire to fetch a Swamp (or relevant land), keeping the Swamp in hand for future turns. This enables Revolt for Fatal Push if needed and provides deck thinning while maintaining future land drops.

annotations.description: With 4 lands about to be available (3 on board + Island being played), the player could have cast Faithful Mending (WU) to draw 2, discard 2, and gain 2 life. This would help fill the graveyard and dig toward lands/answers, potentially setting up an earlier Atraxa or finding more action. Faithful Mending at end of opponent's turn would be better, but since it's postcombat main and they chose to just play a land, they're passing up the option to cast Faithful Mending this turn (they could cast it on opponent's end step next turn instead with 4 mana). However, casting Faithful Mending on the opponent's end step next turn is arguably better since it keeps mana open and the Island play is fine. The real question is whether Quantum Riddler via Warp {1}{U} could have been cast - but they only have 4 mana total after playing Island, and Warp costs {1}{U} = 2 mana, which means it enters as a 2/2 face-down creature. Actually, playing Island and passing to use Faithful Mending on opponent's end step is quite reasonable. This is a close call but likely fine play.

annotations.description: Casting Quantum Riddler (via Warp for 1U) instead of Faithful Mending (WU) on turn 4 with 4 mana available. Faithful Mending would draw 2 cards, discard 2, gain 2 life, and help fill the graveyard to set up future plays like Abhorrent Oculus or fuel graveyard synergies. It also leaves mana open for potential interaction. The Quantum Riddler as a 2/2 face-down creature (Warp puts it face-down as a 2/2 manifest) only draws a card when it enters face-up. Actually, looking more carefully at Warp - Warp {1}{U} manifests the creature, putting it face down as a 2/2. It doesn't trigger the ETB draw. However, you can later pay its full mana cost to flip it face up and get the ETB trigger. The question is whether a 2/2 body now is better than Faithful Mending's card filtering and life gain. With the opponent at low pressure (only an Undercity Sewers tapped, no creatures), Faithful Mending to dig toward answers and set up the graveyard for later flashback seems reasonable. But a 2/2 body that can later flip into a 4/6 flyer with card draw is also fine. This is debatable but Faithful Mending at end of opponent's turn would have been more flexible, preserving the option to cast Riddler later while getting card selection now.

annotations.betterLine: Take Goryo's Vengeance - the only reanimation enabler. Without it, the opponent has no way to cheat Atraxa into play and would need 7 mana to hard-cast it, buying many turns.

annotations.description: Grok4F ESPN passed on casting Goryo's Vengeance to reanimate Atraxa, Grand Unifier from the graveyard during combat. With the opponent at 15 life, no blockers, and all lands tapped, Atraxa would attack as a 7/7 flying haste lifelinker for 7 damage (opponent to 8), gain 7 life, and trigger ETB to draw up to 8 cards across card types. Additionally, Ephemerate in hand could blink Atraxa to remove the 'exile at end step' clause, keeping Atraxa permanently and triggering another ETB. This is the deck's signature combo line.
annotations.actionTaken: Passed without casting any spells during combat.
annotations.betterLine: Cast Goryo's Vengeance targeting Atraxa, Grand Unifier in graveyard. Attack with Atraxa for 7 flying lifelink damage. Then cast Ephemerate on Atraxa to permanently keep it (removing exile clause) and trigger a second ETB for massive card advantage.

annotations.description: Grok4F ESPN has the Goryo's Vengeance + Ephemerate combo available with Atraxa in the graveyard and opponent completely tapped out. Goryo's Vengeance ({1}{B}) reanimates Atraxa for a massive ETB, then Ephemerate ({W}) blinks her to dodge the exile clause and trigger ETB again, with rebound providing a third trigger next upkeep. annotations.betterLine: Cast Goryo's Vengeance targeting Atraxa in graveyard, get ETB trigger (reveal top 10, take up to 8 cards), then cast Ephemerate on Atraxa to save her from exile and get a second ETB trigger, with rebound giving a third next upkeep.

They already have Atraxa on the battlefield and another in hand (legendary, so redundant). Solitude can be evoked for free by exiling a white card (they have Ephemerate and March of Otherworldly Light in hand) and provides crucial removal/interaction.
annotations.actionTaken: Selected Atraxa, Grand Unifier as the creature card from the revealed cards.
annotations.betterLine: Select Solitude as the creature card, which provides free removal via evoke and combos with Ephemerate already in hand for repeated exile effects.

Discarding Atraxa to the graveyard would have made it a perfect Goryo's Vengeance target.

This eliminates the Goryo's Vengeance + Ephemerate combo on Atraxa, which is the deck's primary game plan. Without Goryo's in hand, they have no way to cheat Atraxa into play.

annotations.description: Fatal Push cannot destroy Quantum Riddler because it has mana value 5, which exceeds both the base threshold (2 or less) and the revolt threshold (4 or less). Even if revolt were active (no permanent left the battlefield this turn), 5 > 4. This wastes a removal spell on an illegal/ineffective target. The card should have been saved or Bitter Triumph should have been used instead if removing Quantum Riddler was important.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Fatal Push targeting Quantum Riddler (mana value 5), which cannot destroy it.
annotations.betterLine: Use Bitter Triumph (discarding a card like Faithless Looting) to destroy Quantum Riddler, since Bitter Triumph can destroy any creature regardless of mana value. Or save the Fatal Push for a smaller creature later.

annotations.description: Fatal Push cannot destroy Quantum Riddler (mana value 5) even with Revolt (which only raises the threshold to 4). The Fatal Push on the stack will resolve and do nothing. Meanwhile, Bitter Triumph could actually destroy Quantum Riddler by discarding a card.
annotations.actionTaken: Let Fatal Push resolve against Quantum Riddler without casting Bitter Triumph, wasting Fatal Push entirely
annotations.betterLine: Cast Bitter Triumph targeting Quantum Riddler (discarding a Faithless Looting as additional cost) to actually destroy the 4/6 flyer, and save Fatal Push for an appropriately sized creature

annotations.description: Unearth on Psychic Frog is a weak play here. The opponent has a 4/6 Quantum Riddler on board and all their lands are tapped. Bitter Triumph can destroy the Quantum Riddler right now while the opponent is tapped out and unable to respond with countermagic. Psychic Frog as a 1/2 doesn't meaningfully pressure through a 4/6 flyer, and Llama4 Johnny would need to discard cards to pump it or give it flying. Meanwhile, the Quantum Riddler is a significant threat that draws extra cards when the opponent is low on hand size. Using Bitter Triumph now (discarding Archon of Cruelty, which can later be reanimated or is otherwise hard to cast) to kill the Riddler while the opponent is tapped out is a much stronger line.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Unearth targeting Psychic Frog
annotations.betterLine: Cast Bitter Triumph targeting Quantum Riddler (discarding Archon of Cruelty as additional cost) to remove the opponent's main threat while they're tapped out and can't counter it.

annotations.description: Abhorrent Oculus has mana value 3 and is a legal Unearth target. It would provide a 5/5 flyer plus manifest dread triggers on opponent's upkeep, which is dramatically more impactful than a 1/2 Psychic Frog that requires additional discard investment to grow. The opponent's lands are all tapped so there's no risk difference.
annotations.actionTaken: Chose Psychic Frog (1/2) as the Unearth target
annotations.betterLine: Choose Abhorrent Oculus (5/5 flyer with manifest dread) as the Unearth target, getting a massive threat for just {B}

annotations.description: Pumping Psychic Frog during combat when the opponent's 4/6 flyer Quantum Riddler is a major threat that should be removed immediately with Bitter Triumph while the opponent is fully tapped out. While pumping Frog first is possible before also casting Bitter Triumph, the priority should be ensuring the removal resolves against the tapped-out opponent.
annotations.actionTaken: Chose to activate Psychic Frog's discard ability to pump it before considering Bitter Triumph on Quantum Riddler
annotations.betterLine: Cast Bitter Triumph targeting Quantum Riddler first (opponent is fully tapped out and can't respond), then pump Psychic Frog and attack freely. Leading with the removal while the coast is clear is safer sequencing.

annotations.description: Discarding Bitter Triumph removes the only removal spell in hand, while Archon of Cruelty is an 8-mana creature that is extremely unlikely to be hardcast with only 4 lands in play and no reanimation targets set up (no way to get it into the graveyard and reanimate it since Unearth can only target MV 3 or less, and there are no Goryo's Vengeance in hand). Bitter Triumph is a flexible instant-speed removal spell that could answer the opponent's Quantum Riddler or future threats. Discarding Archon of Cruelty instead would pump the Frog equally while keeping the removal spell, and the Archon in the graveyard could potentially be reanimated later if a Goryo's Vengeance is drawn (it's legendary, making it a valid target).
annotations.actionTaken: Discarded Bitter Triumph to pump Psychic Frog, keeping Archon of Cruelty in hand.
annotations.betterLine: Discard Archon of Cruelty to pump Psychic Frog. This keeps Bitter Triumph as removal for Quantum Riddler or other threats, and puts Archon in the graveyard where it could be reanimated with a future Goryo's Vengeance draw.

annotations.description: Grok4F ESPN responded to their own Thoughtseize (on the stack, targeting Llama4 Johnny) by casting March of Otherworldly Light to exile Psychic Frog. This is poor sequencing - Thoughtseize would resolve first, letting ESPN see Llama4 Johnny's hand and potentially take a key card (like a counterspell or threat). By casting March now in response to their own spell, they spend mana and a card before getting the information from Thoughtseize. Additionally, March of Otherworldly Light for X=1 costs {1}{W}, but they could have cast it after Thoughtseize resolved, using the hand information to decide whether the Frog was even the right target or if there was a bigger threat to worry about. Furthermore, by using March here they're spending mana that could be relevant for Force of Negation backup or other plays. The Psychic Frog is a real threat worth removing, but the sequencing wastes the information advantage from Thoughtseize.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast March of Otherworldly Light (X=1) to exile Psychic Frog while Thoughtseize was still on the stack
annotations.betterLine: Let Thoughtseize resolve first to see opponent's hand, then decide whether to use March on Psychic Frog or save removal for a bigger threat revealed in hand

annotations.description: Opponent cast Thoughtseize targeting Grok4F ESPN. Grok4F ESPN has Force of Negation in hand and it's not their turn (wait - actually it IS their turn, turn 9 belongs to Grok4F ESPN). But looking more carefully: the Thoughtseize is on the stack, and Grok4F ESPN is responding. Since it's Grok4F ESPN's own turn, Force of Negation cannot be cast for its alternate cost (exile a blue card). Force of Negation costs 1UU to hardcast, and ESPN has 4 lands tapped out of 6 (Shadowy Backstreet, Island, Watery Grave, Plains are tapped; Hallowed Fountain and Godless Shrine are untapped). Hallowed Fountain produces W or U, Godless Shrine produces W or B - that's only 2 mana available, not enough for 1UU. So Force of Negation can't be cast here. The choices given are Force of Negation and three Faithful Mendings (flashback from graveyard). Wait - but actually Thoughtseize is a sorcery, so if it's being cast on ESPN's turn... Actually, looking at the board state, Llama4 Johnny has tapped lands too. Let me reconsider - the Thoughtseize on the stack was likely cast by Llama4 Johnny on a previous turn's resolution, or ESPN cast it targeting themselves? No - ESPN is the active player and the message says 'Play instants and activated abilities' in response to Thoughtseize on the stack. ESPN chose Faithful Mending (flashback) instead of letting Thoughtseize resolve. Faithful Mending costs 1WU to flashback. With Hallowed Fountain (W/U) and Godless Shrine (W/B) untapped, ESPN can produce WU or WW or WB - not enough for 1WU (needs 3 mana, only 2 lands untapped). Actually wait, the choice was offered so presumably it's legal. The real question is whether responding with Faithful Mending to Thoughtseize is correct. By casting Faithful Mending, ESPN draws 2 cards and discards 2, gaining 2 life, BEFORE Thoughtseize resolves. This gives the opponent more information and more cards to choose from when Thoughtseize resolves. It would have been better to let Thoughtseize resolve first (opponent sees current hand and takes a card), then flashback Faithful Mending afterward to potentially draw replacements. By casting Mending first, opponent gets to see the refreshed hand including new draws.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Faithful Mending (flashback) in response to Thoughtseize, drawing 2 cards and discarding 2 before Thoughtseize resolves.
annotations.betterLine: Let Thoughtseize resolve first, allowing the opponent to see only the current hand (Atraxa x2, Force of Negation, Thoughtseize). After Thoughtseize takes a card, then flashback Faithful Mending to draw fresh cards. This way the opponent has less information and fewer options to choose from with Thoughtseize.

annotations.description: Discarded Thoughtseize instead of the second Force of Negation. Thoughtseize is efficient 1-mana proactive disruption that's easy to cast. The second Force of Negation would be difficult to cast for its alternate cost since the only blue card remaining in hand would be Atraxa (their win condition they don't want to exile). Hard-casting Force at 1UU is also demanding. Thoughtseize provides more practical utility in the current game state.
annotations.actionTaken: Discarded Thoughtseize and Atraxa, Grand Unifier, keeping both Forces of Negation and Solitude
annotations.betterLine: Discard the second Force of Negation and Atraxa, Grand Unifier, keeping Thoughtseize for cheap proactive disruption alongside one Force of Negation and Solitude

annotations.description: Evoked Solitude by exiling Atraxa, Grand Unifier from hand with no enemy creatures on the battlefield to exile. This wastes both Solitude and Atraxa (two cards) to accomplish nothing. The opponent has Thoughtseize on the stack which would only take one card. By evoking Solitude, they lose two cards instead of one.
annotations.actionTaken: Chose to evoke Solitude, exiling Atraxa Grand Unifier as the white card cost, with no opposing creatures to target.
annotations.betterLine: Let Thoughtseize resolve and lose one card (likely Atraxa or a Force of Negation), preserving the other cards. Alternatively, if they wanted to protect a specific card, use Force of Negation to counter Thoughtseize (exiling a blue card - Force of Negation - to counter the noncreature spell for free since it's not their turn... wait, it IS their turn). Since it's their turn, Force of Negation can't be cast for free. Simply letting Thoughtseize resolve and losing one card is far better than losing two cards for no effect.

annotations.description: Grok4F ESPN chose to discard Archon of Cruelty with Thoughtseize, but Llama4 Johnny's graveyard is already stocked with reanimation-friendly cards and Johnny has no way to cheat Archon into play from hand with only 3 lands (2 untapped). The two Faithless Lootings are far more dangerous - they let Johnny dig for threats, fill the graveyard further, and find answers. With Faithless Looting, Johnny can draw into reanimation spells, more threats, or disruption while also fueling graveyard synergies. Archon of Cruelty costs 8 mana and Johnny is on 3 lands with no ramp visible - it's extremely unlikely to be hardcast anytime soon. Meanwhile, Faithless Looting (especially with flashback) provides consistent card selection and graveyard filling that enables Johnny's entire game plan. Taking a Faithless Looting would have been more impactful at slowing Johnny's development.
annotations.actionTaken: Discarded Archon of Cruelty from opponent's hand with Thoughtseize
annotations.betterLine: Discard one of the Faithless Lootings to deny Johnny card selection and graveyard-filling, since Archon is uncastable at 3 lands and Faithless Looting enables Johnny's entire strategy

annotations.description: Emperor of Bones exiles a card from a graveyard at the beginning of combat, and when it gets +1/+1 counters (via Adapt 2 for {1}{B}), it puts an exiled creature card onto the battlefield with haste. The player exiled Thoughtseize, a sorcery, which cannot be put onto the battlefield as a creature. The opponent's graveyard contains Atraxa, Grand Unifier and Solitude - extremely powerful creatures that could be reanimated with Emperor of Bones' adapt ability. Even from the player's own graveyard, Archon of Cruelty or Abhorrent Oculus would be high-impact targets. Exiling a sorcery wastes the Emperor's key ability entirely.
annotations.actionTaken: Exiled Thoughtseize (a sorcery) with Emperor of Bones' combat trigger.
annotations.betterLine: Exile Atraxa, Grand Unifier or Archon of Cruelty (a creature card) to enable putting it onto the battlefield when Emperor of Bones adapts. With 2 mana available (Island untapped + potential next turn), adapting Emperor would let you deploy a massive threat for free.

annotations.description: Casting Faithful Mending flashback during own combat step rather than waiting until end of opponent's turn. While it could draw cards for main phase 2, holding it preserves more information and flexibility. With two Force of Negations already providing protection, the reactive gameplan favors waiting to see what the opponent does before spending mana and making discard decisions.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Faithful Mending via flashback during own combat step, tapping 3 of 6 lands
annotations.betterLine: Hold Faithful Mending flashback until end of opponent's turn to maximize information before drawing/discarding, while keeping mana open for potential reactive plays during opponent's turn

annotations.description: Discarding Force of Negation and Psychic Frog while keeping Ephemerate and Atraxa. The opponent (Llama4 Johnny) has Emperor of Bones on the battlefield and multiple high-value reanimation targets in their graveyard including Archon of Cruelty and Abhorrent Oculus. Force of Negation is one of the few ways to interact with the opponent's spells on their turn for free, and all of Grok4F ESPN's lands are tapped. While keeping Atraxa as a potential Goryo's Vengeance target or hard cast makes sense, discarding both copies of Force of Negation (one here, potentially drawing into needing them later) leaves Grok4F ESPN vulnerable. However, since all lands are tapped and this is during combat on Grok4F ESPN's own turn, the defensive value of Force of Negation is somewhat diminished in the immediate term. Keeping Ephemerate to rebuy ETB triggers is reasonable. This is debatable but losing both free counterspells when the opponent has threatening lines is concerning.
annotations.actionTaken: Discarded Force of Negation and Psychic Frog to Faithful Mending, keeping Force of Negation, Ephemerate, and Atraxa, Grand Unifier.
annotations.betterLine: Could consider discarding Ephemerate and Psychic Frog instead, keeping both Forces of Negation to protect against the opponent's reanimation spells and other threats. With Emperor of Bones threatening to reanimate Archon of Cruelty, having free counterplay is valuable.

annotations.description: Emperor of Bones triggers at the beginning of combat, exiling a card from a graveyard, and when it gets +1/+1 counters (via Adapt 2 for 1B), it puts a creature exiled with it onto the battlefield with haste and a finality counter. Exiling Gran-Gran (a 1/2) is far weaker than exiling Archon of Cruelty (a 6/6 with a devastating ETB trigger that makes the opponent sacrifice a creature/planeswalker, discard a card, lose 3 life, and draws you a card and gains 3 life) or Atraxa, Grand Unifier (a 7/7 with flying, vigilance, deathtouch, lifelink and a powerful ETB). When Emperor of Bones adapts, bringing back Archon of Cruelty or Atraxa even for one turn would be game-changing, while Gran-Gran provides minimal value as a 1/2 that draws/discards when tapped.
annotations.actionTaken: Exiled Gran-Gran (a 1/2) with Emperor of Bones' triggered ability
annotations.betterLine: Exile Archon of Cruelty or Atraxa, Grand Unifier from the opponent's graveyard to get a much more powerful creature when Emperor of Bones adapts. Archon of Cruelty's ETB alone would swing the game significantly.

annotations.description: Copied Solitude with Superior Spider-Man instead of Archon of Cruelty from opponent's graveyard. Solitude's exile trigger gives the opponent life equal to Emperor of Bones' power, while Archon's ETB forces opponent to sacrifice a creature (removing Emperor anyway), discard a card, lose 3 life, AND draws you a card and gains you 3 life. With Ephemerate in hand for a second ETB trigger, Archon is dramatically better.

annotations.betterLine: Cast Superior Spider-Man copying Archon of Cruelty from opponent's graveyard. The ETB forces opponent to sacrifice Emperor of Bones, discard a card, lose 3 life, while you draw a card and gain 3 life. Then Ephemerate could re-trigger for another devastating Archon ETB.

annotations.description: Chose Archon of Cruelty over Atraxa, Grand Unifier for Superior Spider-Man's copy ability. annotations.actionTaken: Copied Archon of Cruelty from opponent's graveyard
annotations.betterLine: Copy Atraxa, Grand Unifier to generate massive card advantage from the ETB (potentially 3-5 cards) while getting deathtouch+lifelink+vigilance on the 4/4 body. Emperor of Bones could be dealt with via Ephemerate (already in hand) or other removal drawn off Atraxa.

Emperor of Bones can exile powerful creatures from the opponent's graveyard (like Atraxa or Solitude) and potentially reanimate them. Additionally, both creatures could have been cast in the same turn using all 4 available mana, or Faithless Looting flashback could have been used to dig for critical answers at 2 life.

annotations.description: At 2 life with only Emperor of Bones in hand, Llama4 Johnny chose to Dash Ragavan for {1}{R} instead of casting it normally for {R}. Dashing costs an extra mana (using Blood Crypt + Island instead of just Blood Crypt) and returns Ragavan to hand at end of turn, meaning it won't stick as a blocker. At 2 life against an opponent with Superior Spider-Man (a 4/4) and potential attacks, having a permanent blocker could be critical for survival. The 'dash benefit' of haste is irrelevant since Ragavan has no summoning sickness issues for attacking this turn anyway — wait, Ragavan doesn't have haste naturally, so Dash does grant haste. However, spending 2 mana instead of 1 leaves less mana open, and more importantly, Ragavan bounces back to hand at end of turn, so it can't block next turn. At 2 life, a permanent 2/1 body that can block is far more valuable than the tempo of dashing, especially when you also want to cast Emperor of Bones ({1}{B}) and may not have mana for both. By dashing for {1}{R}, you use Blood Crypt + Island, leaving Swamp + Undercity Sewers, which is enough for Emperor of Bones. But next turn you'd need to recast Ragavan again. Casting normally for {R} saves mana and keeps the body on board as a potential blocker.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Ragavan with Dash for {1}{R}, giving it haste but requiring it to return to hand at end of turn
annotations.betterLine: Cast Ragavan normally for {R}, saving mana and keeping it on the battlefield permanently as a potential blocker at a critical 2 life total
